children: Polish interest rates could remain unchanged this year, but a rate increase in 2026 cannot be ruled out if a pick-up in inflation proves persistent, central banker Henryk Wnorowski told Reuters.
The National Bank of Poland kept its main interest rate at 3.75% last week, maintaining its cautious approach as rising commodity prices and increased energy costs create a risk of higher inflation.
After that, NBP Governor Adam Glapinski said Poland's central bank was in wait-and-see mode, and interest rates may remain unchanged until the middle of next year.

"I see a chance that interest rates could remain unchanged this year. However, given the highly dynamic nature of the external environment and the loose fiscal policy in our country, I do not rule out the possibility of a hike," Wnorowski said.

"This could happen if inflation readings were to settle consistently above the upper limit of the target deviation range, that is a real risk, although I remain an optimist," the MPC member said in an interview with Reuters.
In August, the price growth rate in Poland accelerated to 3.4% year-on-year, from 3.0% in July, just below the 3.5% upper limit of the inflation target range.
"There are strong indications that CPI will move out of this range as early as September," said Wnorowski, adding that this would not automatically imply a rate hike in October.

"This is a prospect that is beginning to cause concern and, at the same time, presents a challenge for the Monetary Policy Council, which will be forced to make more difficult decisions in light of this new situation."
Wnorowski said the key issue was determining whether higher inflation was a "permanent" phenomenon or "incidental" phenomenon.
The Polish central bank publishes inflation and growth projections three times a year, in March, July and November. The forecasts are an important input for MPC decisions on interest rates.

"If a scenario were to unfold in which the November projection shows a sustained rise in inflation, then in my view, the Council would not hesitate to raise interest rates," said Wnorowski, adding that the arguments for tightening monetary policy have increased.
The MPC member said that another factor that could influence the Council's decision is the draft budget for 2027, which points to a continuation of "extremely loose" fiscal policy.
"This must have consequences for monetary policy, which in such a situation must inevitably be more restrictive," Wnorowski said.

He expects inflation to exceed the NBP target range in September
